title: Bytecode and its benefits
context: What is bytecode, and what are its benefits?

source.title: JavaGuide (Snailclimb): Java basics questions (1 of 3)
source.note: Question and topic from this JavaGuide article. The answer is an original English write-up; see content/sources/javaguide/NOTICE.md.

answer: Bytecode is the platform-neutral instruction set that `javac` produces from Java source, stored in .class files. Any machine with a JVM can run it, so the same build runs on Linux, macOS or Windows. The JVM also verifies bytecode before running it, which protects against unsafe code, and the JIT compiler can optimise hot paths at runtime. The trade-off is a small startup cost and the need for a JVM.

points.title: Platform independence
points.why: One compiled artifact runs on any JVM, which is the core promise of Java.

points.title: Verification and safety
points.why: The JVM checks bytecode before running it, so malformed or unsafe code is rejected.

points.title: Runtime optimisation
points.why: The JIT compiler turns hot bytecode into native code while the program runs.
